title: Filipino justice--from concept to practice
primary_topics: Doctrine of separation of powers as basic constitutional framework
1994 SC precedent upholding pork barrel -- and why changed facts make it inapplicable now
What makes the current PDAF law unconstitutional
Three routes to abolish pork barrel: SC unconstitutionality, congressional repeal, people's initiative
sub_topics: Three-branch division: Congress legislates, President executes, SC interprets
Marcos PD-era and Cory revolutionary EO-era as exceptions (decrees and EOs still valid unless repealed)
Judicial legislation as anathema to Constitution
Two prohibited legislative roles: (1) specifying projects, (2) determining offices/NGOs to receive funds
1994 precedent: legislators only 'recommended' projects; executive retained absolute discretion
Change-in-facts doctrine: stare decisis doesn't apply when facts change
Constitutional path -- legislators may include specific projects in the law itself (e.g. specific bridge, university)
Unconstitutional path -- lump-sum + post-enactment legislator discretion to direct it
Bogus NGOs and ghost projects as criminal misuse
Hospitals, bridges, roads, scholarships, emergency aid still fundable through line agencies
People's initiative path: Lambino vs Comelec (Oct 25 2006, J Carpio during CJ's term) restricted initiative to simple amendments, not complicated revisions
Initiative procedural requirements: 12 percent of 50 million voters; 3 percent in each of 234 districts; Comelec approval; referendum; appealable to SC -- at least a year, longer if SC-tested
Closing line: 'If these two solutions are ignored, it is time for another Edsa'

stances.claim: Under separation of powers, Congress legislates, President executes, SC interprets -- and the delineation is 'exclusive and absolute,' with the only historical exceptions being abrogations of the Constitution itself (Marcos PDs, Cory EOs).
stances.rhetorical_move: doctrinal-foundation framing (re-establishing first principles before the analytical move)

stances.claim: The 1994 SC precedent upholding pork barrel does NOT control the current PDAF case because the underlying fact has changed: the 1994 law made legislator recommendations non-binding, while the current law allegedly makes them binding -- and stare decisis does not apply when facts change.
stances.rhetorical_move: change-in-facts doctrine deployment (using a precedent-distinguishing principle to neutralize the controlling case)

stances.claim: The constitutional path for legislators to fund specific projects is to include them in the law itself (e.g. 'a bridge here, a hospital there') without retaining post-enactment discretion; the unconstitutional path is lump-sum appropriation paired with legislator power to direct it.
stances.rhetorical_move: constitutional/unconstitutional path distinction (offering a permitted alternative to a prohibited practice)

stances.claim: There are three routes to abolish pork barrel -- SC unconstitutionality declaration, congressional repeal, and people's initiative -- but the first two are far less convoluted; the third faces the Lambino doctrine's amendment-vs-revision hurdle plus extreme procedural burdens (12 percent of 50M voters, 3 percent per district, Comelec, referendum, SC review).
If neither the SC declares unconstitutionality nor Congress repeals, then 'it is time for another Edsa' -- a sharp escalation to extra-constitutional people-power as the residual remedy.
stances.rhetorical_move: EDSA-as-residual-remedy invocation (escalating the closing register from doctrinal to revolutionary)

notable_anecdotes: CJ's parenthetical authorial signature on Lambino vs Comelec -- '(Oct. 25, 2006, penned by Justice Antonio T. Carpio during my term as chief justice)' -- the rare moment where he claims institutional ownership of a doctrine that now constrains the people's-initiative route. The dating itself is the credential.

The dual-era exception: Marcos PDs and Cory EOs as the only historical exceptions to the separation-of-powers rule, with the surprising legal note that those decrees and orders remain valid law today unless subsequently repealed. The constitutional asymmetry survived the political eras.

The closing line 'it is time for another Edsa' -- the most extra-constitutional escalation in any of the pork-barrel columns, breaking from doctrinal register into revolutionary-residual remedy register.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban offers a 'Pork Barrel 101' from doctrinal first principles: under separation of powers, Congress legislates, the President executes, and the Supreme Court interprets -- 'exclusive and absolute,' with the only historical exceptions being constitutional abrogations (Marcos PDs and Cory EOs, whose issuances remain valid unless subsequently repealed). Legislators are prohibited from two acts: specifying particular projects and determining which agencies or NGOs receive funds from a lump sum. He explains that the 1994 SC precedent upholding pork barrel is distinguishable because the controlling fact has changed: the 1994 law treated legislator recommendations as non-binding, while the current PDAF allegedly makes them binding -- and 'stare decisis would not apply when the facts change.' The constitutional path: legislators may include specific projects in the law itself (a particular bridge, hospital, university). The unconstitutional path: lump-sum appropriation paired with post-enactment legislator discretion. Reported diversions to 'bogus NGOs and ghost projects' add criminal misuse to constitutional infirmity. He maps three abolition routes: SC unconstitutionality declaration, congressional repeal, and people's initiative -- but the third faces Lambino vs Comelec (Oct 25, 2006, J Carpio, 'during my term as chief justice'), which restricts initiative to amendments not revisions, plus procedural burdens (12 percent of 50M voters, 3 percent per district, Comelec, referendum, SC review). He concludes that SC-unconstitutionality or congressional-repeal routes are 'less convoluted and much faster,' closing with the rare escalation: 'If these two solutions are ignored, it is time for another Edsa.'
